![Terence Tao, who sees AI as the catalyst for an era of "big mathematics." Image from [IEEE Spectrum](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-in-mathematics).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[IEEE Spectrum](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-in-mathematics) surveys how working mathematicians are reacting as AI systems start to conjecture, prove, and formalize, and finds the community split over what its own role should become.

What the article reports:

- Recent milestones: gold-medal performance at the [International Mathematical Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Mathematical_Olympiad) by [Google DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/) and [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) systems, DeepMind's Aletheia autonomously producing a publishable PhD-level result in arithmetic geometry, an OpenAI model disproving a combinatorial-geometry conjecture, and [Math, Inc.](https://www.math.inc/)'s Gauss formalizing the 24-dimensional case of [Maryna Viazovska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryna_Viazovska)'s sphere-packing proof in two weeks.

- Three camps are emerging: AI as a tool (human understanding matters most), AI as a partner (shared discovery), and AI as an oracle (only the answers matter).

- The researchers the piece interviews divide along that split:
    - [Yang-Hui He](https://lims.ac.uk/yang-hui-he/) (London Institute for Mathematical Sciences) voices the oracle worry: if machines hand down answers no one grasps, human mathematicians could become "priests to oracles."
    - [Akshay Venkatesh](https://www.math.ias.edu/~akshay/) (Princeton, Fields Medalist) takes the human-centric view he first pressed at his 2022 Fields Medal Symposium, asking not just what computers can do but what mathematics is *for* — for him numbers are "a way of bringing us to agreement," and he worries the years-long struggle to understand a proof may become hard to justify to funders and to mathematicians themselves.
    - [Maia Fraser](https://frasermaia.github.io/) (University of Ottawa) shares that stance: even when a machine settles a question, coming up with "an elegant, beautiful human proof" remains "a valuable endeavor," because the struggle to understand is one of the discipline's greatest rewards.
    - [Terence Tao](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tao/) (UCLA, Fields Medalist) is the collaborative voice: his "big mathematics" is large decentralized human-AI projects where formalization in proof assistants like [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/) establishes trust through verification rather than reputation, so an idea from an unknown or an amateur counts if the formal proof checks.

- The risks the piece names: *accessibility* (math becoming compute-gated and elitist), *motivation* (why spend years understanding what a machine can produce?), and *intellectual atrophy* in students who skip the struggle.

## My Notes

- **Understanding is the step AI leaves behind**: Tao has [split doing mathematics into generation, verification, and digestion](/posts/20260422-proof-generation-vs-digestion/) — producing a proof, checking it, and actually understanding it. AI is fast at the first two and slow at the third. The article's motivation worry is that last gap: if a machine can hand you a checked proof, the years of effort spent understanding it start to look optional, felt as a loss of purpose rather than a missing capability.

- **The elitism risk cuts against an open-weight counter-trend**: the article's worry is that compute-gated frontier models make math pay-to-play, inverting a discipline that needed only pen, paper, and training. That holds only if the useful systems stay proprietary. [Open-weight models have stayed close behind the frontier](/posts/20260627-open-weights-frontier-gap/), so whether math becomes elitist depends on how wide the proprietary gap grows. The risk is real but conditional.

- **Verification covers only the proof step**: formalization catches errors at the proof step, which is why Tao says it "filters out a lot of the rubbish." But the trust chain still includes whether the formal statement faithfully captures the informal one, and whether the checker itself is sound. A Claude agent once [found a buffer overflow in the Lean runtime under formally verified code](/posts/20260413-verified-not-safe/), so even "checked in Lean" leaves the formalization and the checker outside the guarantee.
